strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: While most zero-shot transfer methods focus on single vision-language models (VLMs), this paper effectively addresses the complementary strengths and weaknesses of vision-only foundation models (VFMs, having fine-grained visual discrimination without semantic alignment) and VLMs (having text alignment but potential modality gap or visual coarseness).

Principled formulation and optimization: Reformulating the multi-model ensemble problem with squared inner products in regularized optimal transport allows a natural minorization-maximization (MM) derivation that adaptively weights models without ground-truth validation labels. The joint co-evolution of GMM clustering parameters for VFMs and the OT transport plan is technically sound.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper conducts extensive experiments across 26 datasets spanning natural images, remote sensing, and computational pathology. Both transductive and inductive test settings are evaluated, yielding significant accuracy improvements over single models and strong test-time adaptation baselines.

Thorough ablation and convergence analysis: The manuscript clearly evaluates the impact of each core component (VFM incorporation, self-adaptive weighting, joint GMM-OT optimization), displays fast convergence within 5-10 iterations, and provides runtime/memory efficiency analysis.
weaknesses: Fairness of multi-model comparisons: In Tables 1 and 4, most baseline methods (e.g., TransCLIP, ADAPT, GTA-CLIP, COSMIC) are evaluated strictly using a single CLIP backbone (ViT-B/16), whereas the top-performing SOTA variants combine CLIP with modern, substantially larger and stronger visual encoders (DINOv2/DINOv3 ViT-L). While the authors include a CLIP-1 + CLIP-2 ablation, comparing against baselines augmented with multi-model feature fusion or ensembling across all natural benchmarks would make the comparative claims stronger.

Sensitivity to class distribution and marginal priors: The entropic optimal transport formulation assumes a target marginal distribution $q \in \Delta^K$, typically set to a uniform distribution $1/K$. In real-world zero-shot scenarios where target datasets exhibit severe class imbalance, enforcing uniform marginal constraints can degrade performance. The paper lacks discussion or empirical analysis regarding robustness under class-imbalanced test distributions.

Details regarding GMM initialization and high-dimensional stability: Fitting Gaussian Mixture Models directly on high-dimensional feature spaces (e.g., $D=1024$ for ViT-L) can suffer from singularity or bad local optima. The paper should explicitly clarify how the initial GMM parameters $\Theta^{(0)}$ are initialized (e.g., initialized using VLM text-aligned pseudo-labels or k-means) and whether covariance regularization is required.

strengths: Compelling motivation: The paper tackles a well-identified limitation in zero-shot classification—namely that VLMs (like CLIP) possess semantic alignment but often lack fine-grained visual discrimination, whereas VFMs (like DINO) provide rich visual cluster structures without text alignment.

Sound mathematical formulation: Formulating multi-model integration through an optimal transport framework with quadratic inner-product terms solved via Minorization-Maximization (MM) is elegant. It naturally leads to an adaptive weighting mechanism that dynamically balances the contribution of each model without requiring labeled validation data.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The method is benchmarked across 26 datasets spanning three diverse domains (natural images, remote sensing, and computational pathology) in both transductive and inductive settings, showing consistent and substantial performance gains.

Practicality and efficiency: SOTA is training-free and backpropagation-free, operates with black-box feature extractors, converges rapidly within 5–10 MM iterations, and demonstrates competitive runtime/memory overhead compared to graph-based transductive baselines.
weaknesses: Fairness of multi-model comparison against single-model baselines: In Table 1, SOTA achieves 77.4% and 77.8% when incorporating DINOv2/DINOv3, which are substantially stronger visual backbones than CLIP ViT-B/16. When restricted to combining CLIP ViT-B/16 and CLIP RN50 (CLIP-1 + CLIP-2), SOTA achieves 72.5%, which is below the single-model baseline GTA-CLIP (74.5%) and on par with ADAPT (72.4%). A comparison where baselines are also adapted to fuse multi-model predictions/features would provide a fairer assessment of the transport plan's architectural advantage.

Class marginal assumption and class imbalance: Standard entropic optimal transport requires specifying the marginal target distribution q. If q is fixed to uniform (1/K), performance can degrade on datasets with severe class imbalance. The paper should explicitly discuss how q is set across datasets and evaluate the robustness of SOTA under imbalanced class distributions.

GMM initialization and high-dimensional behavior: Fitting GMMs on high-dimensional visual representations (e.g., D=768/1024) across large category counts (e.g., ImageNet K=1000) can suffer from degenerate clusters or numerical sensitivity. The exact initialization strategy for the GMM parameters (presumably initialized via VLM zero-shot posterior predictions) and covariance regularization details should be made explicit in the main text.
Minor notation inconsistency: In Equation (19) in the Supplementary Material, the denominator uses \sum_i Q_{ic}^{(t)} instead of \sum_i T_{ic}^{(k+1)}, which appears to be an uncorrected typo.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: leveraging the complementary strengths of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) for zero-shot classification in a training-free manner.

The empirical evaluation is extensive in terms of domain coverage, spanning 26 datasets across natural images, remote sensing, and medical histopathology under both transductive and inductive settings.
The iterative Minorization-Maximization (MM) and Sinkhorn algorithm formulation is computationally efficient and shown empirically to converge within a few iterations.
weaknesses: Unfair capacity comparison against published baselines: In Table 1 (transductive) and Table 4 (inductive), existing methods (e.g., GTA-CLIP, ADAPT, COSMIC) are evaluated strictly using CLIP ViT-B/16. When SOTA is evaluated using the comparable CLIP-1 + CLIP-2 (ViT-B/16 + RN50) setup, it actually underperforms existing single-model methods (72.5% vs. 74.5% for GTA-CLIP in Table 1; 71.5% vs. 73.3% for COSMIC in Table 4). SOTA only outperforms them when combined with significantly larger and stronger vision backbones (DINOv2 ViT-L/14 and DINOv3 ViT-L/16). Existing methods are not evaluated with equivalent multi-backbone ensembles or larger vision features.

Marginal benefit of the central 'Self-adaptive' mechanism: The core methodological premise is the self-adaptive weighting induced by squaring the inner product in Eq. (7). However, the ablation study in Figure 4 reveals that the performance gain of the self-adaptive mechanism over fixed/non-adaptive weighting is negligible (+0.2% on natural images, +0.3% on remote sensing, and +0.8% on medical datasets). Most of the actual gains appear to originate simply from adding high-capacity DINO features and iterative GMM alignment rather than the proposed adaptive transport formulation.

Missing critical details on GMM initialization and semantic alignment: Unsupervised VFMs possess no text alignment, meaning a standard GMM over VFM visual features suffers from label permutation ambiguity (cluster indices do not correspond to class categories). While the text hints that the joint optimization aligns them, the paper does not specify how $\Theta^{(0)}$ or $T^{(0)}$ are initialized in Algorithm 1 to establish the correct semantic mapping. This omission is critical for technical reproducibility.

Notational sloppiness and mathematical inconsistencies: In the supplementary derivations, Eq. (19) contains an undefined variable $Q_{ic}^{(t)}$ in the denominator (presumably intended to be $T_{ic}^{(k+1)}$). Furthermore, in Eq. (16)–(18), the Sinkhorn scaling vectors are denoted by $p \in \mathbb{R}^K$ and $q \in \mathbb{R}^N$, which inverts the dimensions and directly conflicts with Section 3.1 where $p \in \Delta^N$ and $q \in \Delta^K$ are defined as the marginal probability constraints.

Sensitivity to class distribution and marginal constraints: Standard entropic OT enforces fixed marginals $q$ (typically uniform $1/K$). The paper does not analyze the impact of class imbalance in real-world test sets, where forcing uniform class marginals can lead to significant degradation or artificial bias.

strengths: Exploring the synergy between vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) and self-supervised vision-only foundation models (e.g., DINOv2) for transductive zero-shot learning is a well-motivated and practically relevant topic.
The empirical evaluation covers 11 diverse image classification benchmarks across two different CLIP backbones (ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50).
The alternating optimization procedure converges quickly in practice (within 3–5 iterations), leading to an efficient training-free inference framework.
weaknesses: Severe mathematical and dimensional inconsistencies in the core formulation: (1) In Eq. (5), the transport polytope is defined with constraints $Q \mathbf{1}_K = \mathbf{1}_N$ and $Q^\top \mathbf{1}_N = \mathbf{1}_K$. Summing the entries of $Q$ under these two constraints implies $\sum_{i,k} Q_{ik} = N$ and $\sum_{i,k} Q_{ik} = K$, which requires $N = K$—an impossible condition in general classification benchmarks where $N \gg K$. The column constraint should reflect the sample-to-class ratio (e.g., $\frac{N}{K} \mathbf{1}_K$). (2) In Eq. (8), $Q^{(t)} = \text{Diag}(u) \exp(...) \text{Diag}(v)$ with $u \in \mathbb{R}^K$ and $v \in \mathbb{R}^N$ is dimensionally invalid for left/right matrix multiplication with an $N \times K$ matrix. (3) In Eqs. (9)–(10), $u^{(s+1)} = \frac{\mathbf{1}_K}{K v^{(s)}}$ attempts to multiply an $N \times K$ matrix $K$ by an $N$-dimensional vector $v$, which is undefined without transposition. Furthermore, the symbol $K$ is severely overloaded as both the number of classes and the Gibbs kernel matrix.

Unfair baseline comparison: In Table 1, OTFusion is compared against methods such as TransCLIP, ECALP, DMN, and TDA. However, all baseline methods exclusively utilize CLIP representations, whereas OTFusion introduces DINOv2 ViT-L/14 (a 300M+ parameter self-supervised model). As revealed in the ablation study (Table 2), running GMM on DINOv2 alone ('DINOv2-only') achieves 74.20% average accuracy, which already surpasses all Table 1 baselines (e.g., ECALP at 70.54% and TransCLIP at 70.33%). Hence, the reported performance improvements over prior SOTA stem predominantly from the stronger visual features of DINOv2 rather than the proposed OT fusion mechanism, making the comparison misleading.

The proposed fusion method is outperformed by the naive baseline: In Table 2, simple feature concatenation ('Concatenation') outperforms OTFusion on 9 out of 11 datasets and achieves a higher overall average (75.54% vs. 74.95%). Despite this, the manuscript claims that OTFusion achieves 'comparable or better results', which contradicts the empirical findings. The justification that concatenating features introduces prohibitive overhead is unconvincing, as concatenating 1D feature vectors before GMM clustering adds negligible computational cost compared to the feature extraction itself.

Assumption of uniform class distribution: By constraining the marginal distributions via optimal transport to assign equal mass to each class, the formulation implicitly assumes class-balanced test sets. The paper does not evaluate or discuss how the method behaves under realistic class-imbalanced test distributions, where strict marginal balance constraints typically degrade performance.

Notational and presentation issues: Equations switch inconsistently between number of classes $C$ and $K$ (e.g., Eqs. 1–3 use $C$, Eqs. 4–12 use $K$). In Eq. (2), the text assumes $z$, but inputs are defined as $v$. Typos are present in the text (e.g., 'Flowers12' on page 7).

strengths: Exploring the synergy between vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) and self-supervised vision-only foundation models (e.g., DINOv2) for transductive zero-shot learning is an interesting and practically relevant direction.
The proposed framework is training-free and operates via iterative GMM-Sinkhorn updates, converging within a few iterations without requiring gradient backpropagation or prompt tuning.
Extensive evaluation across 11 diverse benchmarks demonstrates solid accuracy numbers and shows stability across hyperparameter ranges for $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparisons: All competing methods in Table 1 (e.g., TransCLIP, ECALP, DMN, TDA, TPT) operate solely with CLIP encoders (ViT-B/16 or ResNet-50). OTFusion introduces a significantly larger external model, DINOv2 ViT-L/14 (~300M parameters). In Table 2, relying predominantly on DINOv2 ('DINOv2-only') already achieves 74.20%, compared to native CLIP at 65.24% and OTFusion at 74.95%. Without providing baselines that also incorporate DINOv2 features, it is difficult to determine whether the performance gains stem from the proposed OT framework or simply from the addition of a strong, large visual foundation model.

Proposed distribution fusion is outperformed by naive feature concatenation: In Table 2, straightforward concatenation of CLIP and DINOv2 features into the GMM yields 75.54% average accuracy, outperforming OTFusion (74.95%) on 9 out of 11 datasets. Despite this, the manuscript claims in Section 'Fusion Strategy Matters' that OTFusion achieves 'comparable or better results,' which is factually contradicted by the reported numbers. This weakens the motivation for the proposed probabilistic fusion mechanism over simple feature concatenation.

Mathematical and conceptual inaccuracies in the Optimal Transport formulation: First, the paper states in the abstract and introduction that OTFusion 'minimizes the transport cost between their respective distributions.' In reality, Eq. (4) and Eq. (7) do not compute optimal transport between two distributions $P$ and $Y$; instead, they compute an entropy-regularized sample-to-class assignment where the cost/profit matrix is simply a linear combination of log-posteriors/scores ($P + \lambda Y$). Second, the transport polytope in Eq. (5) is defined as $\mathcal{Q} = \{ Q \in \mathbb{R}_+^{N \times K} \mid Q\mathbf{1}_K = \mathbf{1}_N, Q^\top\mathbf{1}_N = \mathbf{1}_K \}$, which is mathematically empty whenever $N \neq K$, because $\sum_{ik} Q_{ik} = N$ from the first condition and $K$ from the second. The class marginal should be scaled by $N/K$. Third, the symbol $K$ is heavily overloaded, denoting both the number of classes (scalar) and the Sinkhorn Gibbs kernel matrix $K = \exp(\dots)$ in Eqs. (8)-(10).

Close similarity to existing transductive methods: The iterative EM/Sinkhorn clustering scheme strongly mirrors recent transductive ZSL frameworks such as TransCLIP (Zanella et al., NeurIPS 2024) and SeLa/SwAV-style assignments. Given that the main delta is swapping/mixing features with DINOv2, the conceptual and technical novelty is somewhat incremental.

strengths: Leveraging the complementary representations of self-supervised Vision Foundation Models (e.g., DINOv2) and Vision-Language Models (e.g., CLIP) is a promising and practically motivated direction for zero-shot recognition.
The proposed method is training-free and demonstrates fast empirical convergence within 3–5 iterations across 11 benchmark datasets.
The paper is generally well-structured and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparisons: In Table 1, OTFusion is benchmarked against zero-shot and transductive methods that rely solely on CLIP (ViT-B/16 or ResNet-50). However, OTFusion incorporates an additional, significantly larger model—DINOv2 ViT-L/14 (over 300M parameters). Comparing a multi-model ensemble leveraging a large-scale ViT-L vision encoder against single-model ViT-B/ResNet-50 baselines is fundamentally asymmetric. Baseline methods such as TransCLIP, ECALP, or TDA are not evaluated with DINOv2 features or comparable model capacity.

Marginal gain over visual baseline and underperformance relative to naive concatenation: In Table 2, 'DINOv2-only' achieves 74.20% average accuracy, whereas OTFusion achieves 74.95% (a modest gain of 0.75%). Crucially, simple feature concatenation achieves 75.54%, outperforming OTFusion on 9 out of 11 datasets and on average. The claim on page 6 that distribution-based fusion achieves 'comparable or better results' than concatenation is contradicted by the paper's own empirical results.

Missing critical baseline: The introduction discusses DINO-assisted prompt learning (Imam et al., 2024) as the most relevant prior work combining CLIP and DINO for zero-shot classification, yet no empirical comparison or discussion of performance against this method is provided.

Mathematical error in the Optimal Transport polytope definition: In Eq. (5), the constraint set is defined as Q 1_K = 1_N and Q^T 1_N = 1_K. Summing the entries of Q via the first condition yields N, whereas the second yields K. Because N (number of test images) != K (number of classes), this constraint is mathematically inconsistent unless properly normalized by sample and class proportions.

Severe notation overloading and inconsistencies: The symbol K is used interchangeably as the number of foundation models (page 3, bottom left), the number of classes (Eq. 5, 8, 9), and the Sinkhorn Gibbs kernel matrix K in Eq. (9) and (10). Furthermore, C and K are used interchangeably for class count throughout Section 3.

Limited methodological novelty over TransCLIP: The core formulation of combining GMM clustering with entropy-regularized Sinkhorn assignment in transductive ZSL closely follows TransCLIP (Zanella et al., NeurIPS 2024); applying this pipeline across features from an additional vision foundation model represents an incremental extension.
